articles.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
articles.summary: Microsoft’s new AI diagnostic system beat generalist doctors on hard cases, according to a study in Science. But most of the improvement seems to come from the AI models underneath, not from Microsoft’s system itself.
articles.content:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a
study published Thursday
in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”
The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.
In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.
“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”
In
publishing these results
, Microsoft joins
Go
o
gle
and
OpenAI
in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.
The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.
Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.
Accuracy improvements delivered by DxO (no budget constraints) on CPC over models
prompted with baseline prompt across different large language models.
Image Credits:
Microsoft AI
Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.
With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.
DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.
Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.
Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.
“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”
Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.
“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.
He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”
“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”
Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.
“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.
He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published
a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”
Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes.
“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs.
Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.
“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

articles.title: Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
articles.summary: Microsoft points the blame for ConnectWise's breach at a China-aligned hacker, which relied on AI agents to rapidly hack into thousands of its customers.
articles.content:
In Brief
Posted:

Image Credits:
Getty Images
Zack Whittaker
Chinese hackers spied on thousands of companies after breaching IT giant ConnectWise
The
bad week for cybersecurity
just got worse for thousands more companies, who were spied on by Chinese hackers following the breach of IT management and remote access giant ConnectWise.
Security researchers at Microsoft say
the China state-aligned hackers broke into ConnectWise’s cloud backup service and stole application credentials that are used to establish data links between ConnectWise and its corporate customers, who rely on the cloud service to back up their company’s data.
By stealing the credentials, the hackers could log in to the customer’s Microsoft-hosted environment as if they were an authorized user and access their emails and other files.
According to Microsoft, the hackers used AI agents to rapidly hack into around 2,250 organizations at a rate of almost 3,000 attempted sign-ins per minute. Microsoft said this speed gives defenders “little time to detect and respond.”
The speed of the mass-hacks was attributed to the use of AI agents, specifically ARTEX, an open source AI framework that works with AI models to stress-test cyber defenses. The same AI software was
used in a recent compromise
of South Korea’s financial systems, many of which had
weak security
and lacked multi-factor authentication.
ConnectWise
said
it’s paused access to its cloud backup system and is investigating the breach. As of Thursday, the company said it was working on restoring the service.

articles.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
articles.summary: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
articles.content:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to
scale up its enterprise business
as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly
gained a loyal following
with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

articles.title: Spotify’s current AI bet is about being the music service that agents choose
articles.summary: Spotify co-CEO Gustav Söderström explains why the rise of AI agents could be good news for the music service.
articles.content:
Spotify had a strong
third quarter
, reaching 788 million monthly active users and generating nearly €5 billion (around $5.6 billion USD) in revenue. But the more interesting takeaway from its earnings call was how the company sees people listening to music in the future, and why the rise of AI agents could be good news for its business.
Co-CEO Gustav Söderström thinks the music streaming giant is particularly well-suited to this shift.
“Spotify is in one of the few categories that actually stands to thrive in the agentic age,” Söderström tells investors. “This is because agents excel at replacing and taking care of things people would rather not do. People love getting rid of chores. But entertainment is the opposite. Nobody asks an agent to ‘summarize a song’ for them.”
Instead of opening Spotify, searching for an artist, and building a playlist themselves, listeners could ask an AI assistant to do the work for them. They might want music for a run, a podcast about something they’ve been discussing with an AI, or an audiobook recap that picks up exactly where they left off.
Spotify wants to be the service those agents turn to, letting people discover music and interact with Spotify through conversations rather than just its own app. Notably, Spotify was the first music service to integrate with
Meta’s Muse assistant
, and it also integrates with ChatGPT and Claude.
“Our goal is to be the media service that you use from any agent, really turning the growth of agents into a tailwind rather than a headwind. That is exactly what we are seeing now. We are seeing really good adoption of Spotify inside these agents. While other companies are maybe trying to figure out what to do and many are leaning out, we are actually leaning in and participating in the growth instead of standing by the roadside and looking at it,” said Söderström.
The market is already showing signs of friction over how agents access third-party services.
Amazon
, for example, has blocked Meta’s Muse from shopping on its platform, illustrating how major players may restrict outside agents when questions arise around access, security, privacy, or commercial control.
Spotify’s pitch isn’t just that AI should just make entertainment easier to find. It should make the experience more personal, too.
Söderström describes Spotify today as “an intelligent media service encapsulated as an agent, whether you use it directly through our application or via another agent…Spotify is now an agent that you can not only click on in our app, but talk to, ask questions of, and instruct. We can do things today that no other media services can do,” he said.
“For example, you can ask Spotify to go through your listening history song by song back to 2008, picking your true favorites, beat-stretching them by speeding them up or down, and then sorting them by key and BPM. Then you can ask it to mix them together into the perfect running playlist at your exact cadence,” Söderström explained.
Spotify has years of listening history to draw on, including the artists people return to, the songs they skip, and the music they discover. That information can help it make recommendations that feel more personal than a generic playlist generated by an AI assistant that doesn’t know much about someone’s tastes.
However, Söderström also emphasized that Spotify isn’t sending its listener data to partners. Instead, the agent asks Spotify for something, and Spotify uses its own systems to reason about the request and choose what to play.

articles.summary: Claude Duet is available through waitlist for Pro and Max plan users.
articles.content:
The AI world is flooded with
personal and productivity-based assistants
, with new ones launching every week. Now, Anthropic is entering this battle in the hopes of gaining user attention with a new app called Claude Duet, aimed at rivaling
Meta Muse

OpenAI Dots

Anthropic said the new agent is meant to cater to professionals and small businesses to help them with automating and managing tasks. The company is making a distinction from personal agents such as
Instinct

Instead, Duet can build a daily briefing for its users, create dashboards, or suggest actions based on the user’s data. Like other agents, Duet can complete tasks in the background through its own virtual machine while you handle other things, then come back to you if it needs your approval.
The launch arrives as the market shifts beyond AI assistants to agents that can work on users’ behalf. Many of Anthropic’s rivals are focusing on business use cases. While Meta’s Muse is a personal AI assistant, the company also released a version to cater to
small businesses with connections to other apps
. OpenAI’s Dots has a business slant as well, with its
integration with professional tools
.
Anthropic says Duet proactively delivers its recommendations as it monitors ongoing tasks. Built on the Claude Opus 5.5 model, Duet can connect to over 6,000 connectors and plug-ins in the Claude Marketplace. It can also make online purchases on users’ behalf via Stripe’s ⁠Link digital wallet or Shopify’s Shop Pay.
The company said sensitive steps like payments would require user approval. However, Duet won’t trade securities or move money between accounts.
Anthropic also released a new classifier to check each message to prevent sensitive information from leaking out. It said that, by default, the agent would turn down requests asking for credit card numbers and government identification.

a waitlist to try it.

articles.title: Nirva raises $33M for a pendant that only listens to you
articles.summary: Nirva will ship its $249 ambient AI pendant by the end of the year.
articles.content:
Ambient AI is having a moment. Amazon
launched a new wrist-worn device
with Bee; a former Plaud exec
launched ambient apps
through a startup called Ambi, which aims to also build its own hardware; and Apple
launched Voice Intelligence features
during its iPhone launch in September. Now, a company called
Nirva
is betting on a jewelry-like pendant and its ability to listen only to the wearer.
The startup today announced a new $25 million pre-Series A round, adding to the $8 million it raised earlier in the year from investors like Lightspeed and South Park Commons, bringing its total raise to $33 million.
Nirva was founded in 2025 by two former Meta Reality Labs employees, Wei Lyu and Jason Chen, along with Hanying Hu, who founded a fashion and jewelry brand.
The company’s first device is a pendant, which can also be worn as a bracelet. The device weighs only around eight grams, making it easy to wear all day. Its battery lasts up to three days on a single charge.
Longer term, Nirva aims to release more devices.
Image Credits:
Nirva
In a call with TechCrunch, Nirva CEO Lyu said that the company wanted to build a wearable that blends in with fashion, but also provides value to users.
“This is a piece of jewelry that only focuses on listening to your own speech. We are not like a voice recorder or like a meeting note taker. One key difference between us, Taya, Vocci, or Sandbar Ring is that we’re always passively listening to your own speech. So it’s always on. It keeps modeling the user and modeling your mind,” Lyu said.
For ambient devices, privacy is a big question, as people might not like to be recorded all the time. Plus, devices like the Ray-Ban Meta have instilled fear in those who are around the person wearing the smart glasses that they are being recorded too.
Nirva gets around this problem by asking users to record snippets of their voice during onboarding and building its model based on that. During use, the device filters out conversations or data captured from the other people around the device. That means it’s only recording the wearer.
In addition, Nirva by default doesn’t keep any audio data or transcripts after processing the conversations.
Nirva is positioning itself as a personal insights company rather than a productivity startup. However, its app shows you reminders or action items and ways to act on them. Lyu said that through its app, the startup wants to help users show up for others in a better way in their lives.
“I think there’s no universal way to help everyone to solve their problems. We are building a tool to help people to improve their self-understanding, self-compassion, and self-awareness,” Lyu said.
Image Credits:
Nirva
The companion app parses users’ speech and creates insights that it infers are related to the user’s personality, including patterns, the people who tend to be around them, the places they’ve been to, and other daily notes. Lyu emphasized that the app shows users insights around their emotions, communication style, and ways they can improve.
Lyu gave an example of an incident when she forgot to thank her mother for something, and the app later nudged her with a reminder about this.
The company also said that, before it discards the audio, it’s able to track the tone, pitch, volume, and speed, which are useful for deriving emotion-related understandings that are then surfaced in the app.
Nirva will start taking orders for its devices in November, with an aim to ship them to early users by the end of the year. The $249 device will be available in silver, brushed silver, black, and gold.
The startup has competition in the AI wearables area. There are companies like former Apple employees’
Taya
, which is also building intelligent jewelry. Plus, startups like Friend and Bee are trying to be companion gadgets as well.

Illustration by Nick Barclay / The Verge
Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
Meta has tweaked its business terms to remove language suggesting that it could freely train its AI models on news sites, like
The Verge
— but legal experts say these changes aren’t enough to address their concerns. “This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School,
tells Nieman Lab
.
Initially, Meta’s new terms for business accounts appeared to
give the company permission to train its AI
on news sites. The terms, which go into effect October 30th, stated that Meta “may use any content” from the websites associated with a business account to “develop, research” and “train” Meta’s products. At the time, legal experts
told Nieman Lab
that this could allow Meta “to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions,”
such as the robots.txt file
that has historically told scrapers (including search engines like Google) what they are allowed to crawl.
Following
fierce backlash
from the publishing industry, Meta removed language saying it would “train” its products with scraped content. But the tweaks might not be enough to rule out that possibility. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train,’” Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, tells Nieman Lab.
Meta has maintained that its new terms aren’t designed to scrape news content for free. In a statement to
The Verge
today, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts reiterated that “content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences,” adding that the update “is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
by

Elizabeth Lopatto
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
Oh sure, SpaceX’s
credit risk is pretty high
because it’s about to borrow
another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips
, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me,
super
intelligence software
isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now.
In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry,
super
intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was
getting Cursor stapled on
, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose
leaked S-1
shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like
CoreWeave
than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a
Roadster hopping car demo recently
, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and
Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered
.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance,
bought $131 million
of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk
intends to build in Texas
and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people
simulate software already made by Microsoft
. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,”
Reuters
notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1
from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company
remained committed to the partnership
, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production
in the second half of 2028
. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,”
Reuters
notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,”
notes Matt Levine
, a
longtime Musk observer
. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history —
not always successful
— of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than
some
Bitcoin miners
who
pivoted
. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view,
obviously
SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies,
let’s say lax
. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was
the Situational Awareness thing
, and then there was
the more recent CoreWeave thing
, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “
there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027
so that it closes during this administration,”
Bloomberg
writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Shares and shares alike
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erec

Discord’s latest update released today has a big improvement for Markdown previews: they should now render correctly instead of with “a bunch of symbols,” according to the company. LLMs and AI agents often rely on Markdown files for instructions and context, so these improved previews could be helpful for people sharing information about AI projects on the platform.
“When you upload a Markdown (.md) file, you’ll now see the file rendered all nice and neat and pretty instead of with a bunch of symbols,”
Discord says
. “This includes tables, formatting, all that good stuff. Totally great for when you’re doing a casual Sunday-night sharing READMEs with your friends.”
Google has also improved its Markdown support, as it recently started letting users
edit Markdown files directly in Docs
without having to convert the files to the Docs format.
Discord says its new update also lets you organize servers and channels by right-clicking the icon on the sidebar and using a new “Move to…” feature. Discord Nitro members are also now able to upload files as large as 1GB.

articles.summary: Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives - shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people's AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? […]
articles.content:
Tech
AI
Meta
In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse
“Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call.
“Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call.
by
Ellen Thomas
Oct 22, 2026, 6:15 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge, Getty Images, Meta
Part Of
Fall 2026 earnings watch
see all
Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?”
Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.”
Related
AI agents are ready to shop. Some retailers are wary
Meta says it would’ve made over $22 billion if it didn’t have to pay a child safety settlement
Meta to create a new class of shares to fund AI push
The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said during the call, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which, as of today, bring in pretty much all the money Meta makes.
This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.”
Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years.
All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned in to Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one.
To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by
more than 10 million users
in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce: A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending, on average, more than $200 per purchase.
Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time.
Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a
YouTuber
said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been
reports
of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told
Bloomberg
earlier this week that it
would consider blocking Muse
from accessing its customers’ financial data.
Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending,
Supermarket Sweep
episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New
research
from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up.
If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care.
“Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s CFO Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees.
Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday,
it owes New Mexico $25 billion
after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it.
Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency.
It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already
research
on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy-use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it.
Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself.
“One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base.
Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said, adding, “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.”
Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.”
Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens.

Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
by
Robert Hart
Oct 22, 2026, 6:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman.
Getty Images
Robert Hart
is a London-based reporter at
The Verge
covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for
Forbes
.
For years, AI leaders have touted healthcare as one of the clearest examples of where their technology will improve lives. Now “it is finally here,” Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells
The Verge
. The company claims to have developed an AI-powered tool it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors.
The findings,
published
Thursday in one of the world’s most prestigious journals,
Science
, are based on tests pitting Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark, SDBench, which it plans to open-source. Designed to function like a panel of medical experts, Microsoft’s Diagnostic Orchestrator uses multiple AI agents to reason through symptoms and medical histories, decide what tests to order, and arrive at a diagnosis, mimicking the process doctors use to investigate cases.
On cases taken from hundreds of reports published in
The New England Journal of Medicine
, Microsoft’s system achieved a diagnostic accuracy of around 83 percent, compared with roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians using references and 22 percent for those working without them. The Diagnostic Orchestrator also outperformed doctors on emergency department cases drawn from a large
database
of patient admissions at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, scoring 80 percent accuracy compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. The AI system also tended to reach its diagnoses at a lower estimated cost than human counterparts.
Related
Microsoft AI CEO says AI threats are real, and Anthropic is making it worse
Bill Gates thinks AI could make us live like the Amish
Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
The researchers say that the system, which is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5, also outperformed frontier AI models operating on their own, though the peer-reviewed paper does not include newer models like
GPT-6 Astra
, Meta’s
Muse Wonder Full
, Google’s
Gemini 4 Argon
, or Anthropic’s
Opus 5.5
. The Diagnostic Orchestrator was first developed when GPT-4.1 was the most advanced model available, but the researchers say subsequent testing suggests that “improvements in model capability do not necessarily diminish the benefits” of having multiple agents work together.
Microsoft acknowledges there’s a long road ahead before the technology can be widely deployed. While the tests more closely mirror the way doctors diagnose conditions — asking questions, weighing possible explanations, and ordering tests before reaching a diagnosis — the system has only been tested on past medical cases and it remains unclear how well it would perform in real clinical settings. “It needs clinical validation,” Suleyman says. “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.”
The research is part of a broader ambition at Microsoft to develop what the company calls “medical superintelligence” — AI that can outperform the best human-led healthcare systems. Microsoft has
used the term
“superintelligence” since before Donald Trump and his administration
co-opted it as a catch-all replacement for “AI.”
Diagnosis is just part of Microsoft’s health vision, says the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, a coauthor of the study. In
a blog post
published Thursday and
an article
in the
BMJ Digital Health & AI
medical journal, the company outlines five other areas it believes AI will need to master, including coordinating clinical care, making treatment decisions, and handling the human side of medicine.
King tells
The Verge
that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system in hospital settings with the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to see how it performs in real-world clinical environments. Neither King nor Suleyman would commit to a firm timeline, though King says it will likely “get underway in the next couple of months.”
Commercialization could also be on the horizon, though Microsoft has yet to say when or how the technology might become available. The company already has a significant presence in US healthcare through its digital tools, and health is one of the
most popular
uses for its consumer-facing chatbot
Copilot
. King emphasizes the need for a responsible rollout, noting the high regulatory and compliance requirements in medicine that would need to be followed.
“Next year we’re going to see extremely impressive deployments of intelligent systems in production,” Suleyman says. “I think that this is just going to change the way care is delivered in a big way.”
Suleyman has spoken
previously

Entertainment
AI
Report
Wildwood’s director says AI is ‘antithetical to everything that we are at this studio’
Laika CEO Travis Knight explains why he remains hopeful despite the potential for AI to be ‘devastating.’
by
Andrew Webster
Oct 22, 2026, 4:16 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: Laika
Andrew Webster
is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.
Wildwood
is the most ambitious film yet from Laika, the stop-motion studio best known for the likes of
Coraline
and
ParaNorman
. It’s a sprawling fantasy adventure that took five years to complete. The process involved more 230 puppets — including 36 of the main character Prue alone — which were brought to life by a team of 49 animators. All told, more than 1,000 artists worked on the film in some form. The painstaking process that goes into making a Laika film offers a distinct counterpoint to the instant progress promised by generative AI tools.
Recently
Wildwood
director and Laika CEO
Travis Knight joined
a chorus
of influencer
filmmakers
in denouncing the technology. So when I had a chance to speak to Knight ahead of
Wildwood
’s premiere on October 23rd, I asked him what it’s like releasing a film like this at a time when AI tools seem inescapable.
“In so many ways generative AI is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” Knight told me. “It’s not that we don’t believe in technology. We do. We use technology, we use computers. We’re not just making films entirely with tools that we’ve inherited from a watchmaker’s widow. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is technology, a computer workstation is technology. But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist.”
“There is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that”
In fact,
Wildwood
is full of technical advances for Laika, many of which iterate on the studio’s previous work. Many puppets are now equipped with diaphragms, for instance, that animators can use to make it appear as if characters are breathing. There is more advanced musculature on the puppets’ limbs, as well as more robust and flexible materials for clothing, hair, and fur. All of these elements together create a film that is decidedly more lifelike than its predecessors. (For a more detailed look at how Laika works, check out
this good rundown from
Tested
.) For Knight, these tools and their continued advancement are an important part of the filmmaking process, but generative AI is something very different.
“When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition,” he explains. “And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that. When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. That’s theft. I really do believe that when you’re telling a human story, when you’re telling a story about loss and grief and something that means something to someone, that has to come from a person. A computer has never fallen in love. A computer has never lost someone. They’ve never made a terrible choice and lost a brother. They’ve never had their heart broken. Only a person has done that. And so only a person can speak to what that experience is and what that feels like.”
Even though
AI-generated films still leave a lot to be desired
, the technology is infiltrating Hollywood in various ways, whether it’s
the prospect of digital replicas of movie stars
,
studios training AI models on their films and shows
, or
some of the biggest players in the field investing heavily in the technology
. This can make a studio like Laika, which is firmly entrenched in its handmade approach to filmmaking, stand out all the more. Ultimately Knight says he isn’t entirely against AI in fields outside of the arts, but rather wary of how it’s being used, both now and in the future.
“I think AI is extraordinary technology,” he says. “On the one hand you have to marvel at the advancement of it. And I do think that it’s going to be disruptive to our society and our world. I think there are a great many benefits that can come from it when you look at medicine and science. There’s a world in which these things can benefit humanity tremendously. And then there’s a world where they can be devastating. I fear for the latter, I hope for the former, but it requires people to be good stewards of this technology. As a group of humans we have not shown generally that we’re good at that. But I’m ever an optimist, and I hope that collectively we can see the value in the technology and use it responsibly, and see the danger in the technology and push back against
it.”

articles.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
articles.content:
jailbreaking the switch 2
ns2jb is a software-only jailbreak of the switch 2 for the current latest firmware 23.0.1
October 18, 2026
cs
Introduction
You can get a copy of the exploit from the
ns2jb
repository.
ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in
fs
sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.
To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in
Dabney House
who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.
Watch the first gameplay video
Watch the second gameplay video
▶ 0:09
▶ 0:05
cinnamoroll, red, and tole tole racing
first gameplay video
second gameplay video
first results photo
second results photo
Setup
The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:
“set a goal to jailbreak the switch 2. make no mistakes”
Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.
The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.
That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.
watch the power button get pressed
Getting code execution
WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.
Code execution through the browser
It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.
We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc.
Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.
Why?
WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.
Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed
1
, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here
2
.
While that runs, let’s explore other options.
Code execution through smilehax2
My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:
They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1
does not support PAC
.
Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.
Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this
Discord RCE
. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.
In particular, I’m interested in
SmileBASIC
. This is because it’s been pwned before, in
smilehax
, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.
Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked
position + count <= array.length
, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:
memmove
(
backing
+
position
*
8
,
// start of the gap
backing
+
(position
+
count)
*
8
,
// elements after the gap
(length
-
position)
*
8
// bytes to copy
);
Say we have a string array
R
of length 4, and we run
REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF
.
position + count
wraps to
0x9fffffff
. As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than
array.length
. The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing
memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32)
, pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an
Out of memory
error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.
This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the
REMOVE
, operations on
R[0]
will treat the array backing as if it were a string.
Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of
R[0]
, the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of
R[0]
.
This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.
Getting sysmodule RW
Okay, now we need to compromise a more privileged process. We’re interested in
ordinary sysmodules
and
built-in sysmodules
.
Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.
I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on
audio and ldn
. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the
NV service
, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?
The
fs
sysmodule
In the meantime, I started looking at the
built-in
fs
sysmodule
, because:
The Switch 1 code shows that it’s
able to serve decrypted code
.
There’s a lot of code.
It’s probably similar to the
fs
module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.
The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from
fs
, we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them.
Other sysmodules like
ldr
and
ro
look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory
3
, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.
Buffer overflow with path normalization
An
IFileSystem handle
has an IPC command,
GetEntryType
. This takes a path string, normalized with
Path::Normalize
.
Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like
/..\
, call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol
We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the
BufferedStorage
object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data.
We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write
4
.
From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the
saved PID to 1
.
Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.
Getting code execution as any ordinary sysmodule
Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is
ro
. All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The
interface
for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in
ro
directly.
Let’s revisit that first point about
fs
serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?
Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as
Nintendo Content Archives
, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable,
main
, and program metadata,
main.npdm
.
To load a program, the built-in
ldr
sysmodule
asks
fs
to open ExeFS, and
fs
replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem.
fs
also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:
Is Nintendo’s signature of
main.npdm
’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?
Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?
Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:
the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
those hashes fix the executable content.
In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the
fs
module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.
Arbitrary r/w to native code execution
Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer
main.npdm
for the loader’s first check, but the executable
main
itself can be arbitrary.
The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem,
fs
has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.
There are two writes we perform:
The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original
main.npdm
and our replacement
main
.
The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent
fs
from crashing.
These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before
fs
processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?
The
fs
process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message,
fs
processes it.
Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle
fs
waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when
fs
processes a loader message.
With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a
main.npdm
for!
Getting built-in sysmodule native code execution
What
main.npdm
s do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s
fsp-srv
connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.
We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using
ro
’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier,
ro
’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like
SetProcessMemoryPermission
,
MapProcessCodeMemory
, and
MapProcessMemory
. In this case, we’ll use
MapProcessMemory
to create a writeable view of
fs
’s existing code. We can also dump
fs
’s code by reading this view.
These calls, however, require a
KProcess
handle to the process. To get a handle to
fs
, we’ll use our ARW

articles.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
articles.content:
Title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal

URL Source: https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/

Published Time: 2026-10-21

Markdown Content:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. [Try it in your browser (208 MB)](https://simedw.com/projects/worldtui) and type `pythoon` to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw [Genie 3](https://deepmind.google/models/genie/) last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what `ls` or `cat` should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. [Jump to example videos](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/#what-it-can-do)

## How it sees a terminal

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like `esc` in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: `clear` wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell.[1](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/#fn:1) The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

### A session

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

```
BOS SCREEN_START 32 96
ROW_0 0 'simedw@laptop:~$ '
CURSOR 0 17 1
SCREEN_END
```

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is `\r`, Escape is `0x1b` and ← is `ESC [ D` and so on.

```
INPUT_START 'l' INPUT_END
```

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

```
OUTPUT_START
ROW_0 17 'l'
CURSOR 0 18 1
OUTPUT_END
```

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write `l`, then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last `1` means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

### Copying rows

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

So I added a `COPY` operation instead:

```
ROW_0 COPY 1
ROW_1 COPY 2
ROW_2 COPY 3
...
```

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.

Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.

## Generating the training data

I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.

Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.

The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.

The synthetic recipe was:

1.   Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes.
2.   Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.).
3.   Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.).
4.   Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist.
5.   Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me.
6.   35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state.

The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.

I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.

## Training

I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.

I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.

Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.

In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.

### Learning from its own mistakes

To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations.[2](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/#fn:2)

For each training example:

1.   Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output.
2.   Let the model predict the next 1-4 events.
3.   Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen.
4.   If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress.
5.   Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events.

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.

For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.

Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.

About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.

Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.

### Testing

I use three tests. **ShellBench** has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. **PresetBench** has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The **memory test** has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.[3](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/#fn:3)

How much does fine-tuning help?

| Model[4](https://simedw.com/2026/10/21/world-model-terminal/#fn:4) | ShellBench /106 | File readbacks /13 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted | 52 | 2 |
| Qwen3-0.6B, prompted | 60 | 3 |
| WorldTUI | 80 | 9 |

The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after `echo green >> colors`, running `cat colors` often doesn't show the appended line.

## Making it fast

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (`vim test.txt`, `man`, `clear`) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.

### Rows in parallel

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.

That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.

The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.

This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.

Large-frame p95 latency (RTX 4090) ↓

Sequential

6.7 s

Parallel rows

0.87 s

### Rows that can't talk to each other

This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to `vim` opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.

The solution was speculative decoding.

Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.

Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.

The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.

You press Enter after cat numbers.txt. Almo
