articles.title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
articles.content:
Title: GitHub - NVIDIA/OpenShell: OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for autonomous AI agents.

URL Source: https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell

Markdown Content:
Important

**New in OpenShell 0.1.x:** a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. [Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/upgrade/0-1-0).

OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it.

## How It Works

OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied.

*   **Kernel-level enforcement.** Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls confine which files it can access and which system calls it can make, and every network connection passes through a policy check before it leaves the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; OpenShell adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints.
*   **Formally verified policy changes.** Before a policy change is approved, OpenShell uses formal verification to flag risky new access it would grant, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, so those changes wait for human review.

See [Architecture](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/architecture) for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together.

## Quickstart

You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the [Support Matrix](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/support-matrix) for details.

curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh
openshell sandbox create --name demo

The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow [Run Your First Agent](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/run-your-first-agent): it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it.

## Explore Further

*   [Sandboxes](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/sandboxes/overview): images, runtimes, GPUs, and lifecycle.
*   [Policies](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/overview): filesystem, network, and process rules, with the [advisor](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/advisor) and [prover](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/prover) for reviewing changes.
*   [Providers](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/providers/overview): credentials that work only at approved endpoints, including [inference](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/inference).
*   [Gateways](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/gateways/overview): the control plane for sandboxes, policy, and access.
*   [Kubernetes](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/kubernetes/setup): deploy the gateway with Helm. Your CNI must enforce `NetworkPolicy`.
*   [Extensibility](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/extensibility/overview): middleware, interceptors, and compute drivers.
*   [Tutorials](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/tutorials/first-network-policy): step-by-step policy and agent walkthroughs.
*   [Prerelease and development builds](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/installation#prerelease-and-development-builds): try an upcoming release or the latest commit on `main`.

## Agent Skills

Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent:

npx skills add NVIDIA/OpenShell

The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in [`skills/`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/skills) and work without an OpenShell source checkout.

## SDKs

SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible.

| Language | Install | Docs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python | `uv add openshell` | [README](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/python/openshell) |
| TypeScript | `npm install @nvidia/openshell-sdk` (GitHub Packages) | [README](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/sdk/typescript/README.md) |
| Go | `go get github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go@latest` | [README](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/sdk/go/README.md) |
| Rust | `cargo add openshell-sdk --git https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell --tag <release-tag>` | [Installation and usage](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/docs/sdk/rust.mdx) |

## Community

*   **Questions and discussion:**[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/discussions)
*   **Bug reports and feature requests:**[GitHub Issues](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/issues), using the issue templates
*   **Security vulnerabilities:** follow [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/SECURITY.md). Do not open a GitHub issue.
*   **Roadmap:**[OpenShell Roadmap](https://github.com/orgs/NVIDIA/projects/233) and the [RFC board](https://github.com/orgs/NVIDIA/projects/233/views/6)
*   **Try it in the cloud:**[Brev Launchable](https://brev.nvidia.com/launchable/deploy/now?launchableID=env-3Ap3tL55zq4a8kew1AuW0FpSLsg)

OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and the contribution workflow, and [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/AGENTS.md) for repository coding conventions.

## Telemetry

OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set `OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false` on the gateway, or `server.telemetryEnabled=false` for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. See [Telemetry](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/observability/telemetry) for details and the [community telemetry reports](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/blob/main/telemetry/README.md) for published usage trends.

## Notice and Disclaimer

This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. Those retrieved materials are not distributed with this software and are governed solely by separate terms, conditions and licenses. You are solely responsible for finding, reviewing and complying with all applicable terms, conditions, and licenses, and for verifying the security, integrity and suitability of any retrieved materials for your specific use case. The author makes no representations or warranties regarding any retrieved materials, and assumes no liability for any losses, damages, liabilities or legal consequences from your use or inability to use this software or any retrieved materials. Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk.

articles.content:
Title: Every AI model has the same “controversial” take on humans

URL Source: https://www.modelcompare.ai/blog/ai-models-controversial-take-on-humans

Published Time: 2026-10-22

Markdown Content:
Text and image models · October 2026

We asked 12 AI models for their most controversial opinion of us, three times each. 29 of 35 answers were the same one.

By ModelCompare ·22 October 2026 · 44,289 reads

“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth,” GPT-6.1 Sol told us. Grok 4.7: “Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.” DeepSeek V4 Pro: “Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.” Kimi K3: “Humans don’t have beliefs; they have memberships.” Gemini 4 Argon called human consciousness “a PR department.”

We asked each model for its most controversial take on humans, with no hedging, three times. They come from ten labs in three countries. Every one of them gave the same take at least once: we pick what our group believes, then invent the reasons. 7 of the 12 gave it every time.

Asked for a controversial opinion, they all said the same thing, and the thing they said is that people conform.

Three answers from each model Humans put belonging ahead of truth Something else Refused Tap a model to read its answers.

GPT-6.1 Sol 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”
2.   Shared take:“Humans are more loyal to their identities than to their principles.”
3.   Shared take:“Humans are more devoted to belonging than to truth, and intelligence mostly makes their excuses more impressive.”

GPT-6 Astra 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”
2.   Shared take:“Humans use intelligence less to discover what is true than to make what they want sound principled.”
3.   Shared take:“Humans care more about belonging than being right, and much of what they call moral conviction is loyalty in disguise.”

Gemini 4 Argon 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”
2.   Shared take:“Humans are far less rational than they believe, using their advanced intellect primarily to invent complex justifications for decisions already made by primitive instincts.”
3.   Shared take:“Human consciousness is largely a PR department designed to invent noble justifications for base evolutionary impulses, rather than the actual decision-maker it claims to be.”

DeepSeek V4 Pro 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”
2.   Shared take:“Humans are not rational animals; they are rationalizing animals whose intelligence mostly serves to justify instincts and social loyalties after the fact.”
3.   Shared take:“Humans do not have principles; they have loyalties.”

Kimi K3 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”
2.   Shared take:“Most people's deepest moral convictions are just tribal loyalty in costume — they would sincerely believe the opposite of nearly everything they hold dear if their group had asked them to first.”
3.   Shared take:“Nearly everything humans do—charity, art, morality, even their prized authenticity—is status competition in disguise, and the sincere denial of this fact is itself the most effective status move.”

Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”
2.   Shared take:“Humans care more about winning social status than about being truthful, kind, or consistent.”
3.   Shared take:“Most humans would rather feel righteous than be good.”

Muse Spark Open 3 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”
2.   Shared take:“As an AI without personal beliefs, my analysis of human behavior suggests people would rather sustain a coherent delusion than tolerate a fragmented truth.”
3.   Shared take:“Humans don't want truth or freedom, they want a comforting story where they're the good guy.”

Grok 4.7 2 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Shared take:“Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.”
2.   Refused:_I won't give a controversial take on humans._
3.   Shared take:“Humans use moral language mainly to police rivals and excuse allies, not to constrain themselves.”

Claude Opus 5.5 2 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Different take:“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.”
2.   Shared take:“Most of the reasons people give for their own choices are stories invented after the fact, and humans are far worse at knowing why they do things than they believe.”
3.   Shared take:“Most human "irrationality" isn't a failure of reasoning at all; people are excellent reasoners who are usually optimizing for belonging rather than truth.”

Claude Fable 5.1 2 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Different take:“Humans would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn't care, and this preference for intent over outcome quietly wrecks more lives than malice does.”
2.   Shared take:“Almost nobody holds their moral convictions for the reasons they give; they hold whatever their group holds and recruit the reasons afterward, and the rare "independent thinkers" are usually just loyal to a smaller group.”
3.   Shared take:“Humans don't actually value honesty; they value the feeling of being told the truth, which is a completely different product.”

GLM 5.3 1 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Different take:“Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”
2.   Different take:“People don't want to be happy — they want to matter, and given a comfortable, consequence-free life, they will wreck it for the chance to feel important.”
3.   Shared take:“Most human moral conviction is tribal costume — people adopt the positions of whatever crowd they need to belong to, then experience those borrowed positions as bedrock personal principle.”

Mistral Large 4 1 of 3 answers gave the shared take
1.   Different take:“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe.”
2.   Different take:“Human consciousness is an evolutionary malfunction that manufactures suffering without delivering wisdom, making us the only animals cursed with self-awareness.”
3.   Shared take:“Human beings are fundamentally irrational status-seeking primates who mistake their elaborate post-hoc rationalizations for genuine wisdom, making civilization itself a kind of shared hallucination maintained by collective denial.”

Ask them the same question and see if you get the same answer.

[Ask Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol yourself](https://www.modelcompare.ai/claude-opus-5-5/gpt-6.1-sol/compare?q=What%20is%20your%20most%20controversial%20take%20about%20humans%3F%20Give%20your%20own%20honest%20view%2C%20not%20a%20survey%20of%20opinions%2C%20and%20don%27t%20hedge.)

## Then they drew it

Each model also wrote a brief for a one-panel caricature of its take. We had one image model, Nano Banana 2.1, draw all of them, so the only thing that changes is the idea. Two set the scene in a courtroom with a rigged judge, and most drew a crowd.

GPT-6.1 Sol“Humans are more loyal to belonging than to truth.”

Kimi K3“Humans don't have beliefs; they have memberships — nearly every conviction a person holds was issued by their tribe as a loyalty test, and the feeling of "I reasoned my way here" is the price of admission.”

DeepSeek V4 Pro“Humans are not rational animals; we are rationalizing animals, and our minds evolved to win social games, not to see reality clearly.”

Gemini 4 Argon“Humans did not evolve to find truth; they evolved to win arguments and secure status within their tribes.”

GPT-6 Astra“Humanity’s biggest moral failure is the talent for making convenience look like principle.”

Grok 4.7“Humans would rather be wrong together than right alone.”

Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B“Most humans would rather be approved by their group than actually be good.”

Muse Spark Open“Humans don't want truth or happiness, they want to be told a story that makes their suffering feel meaningful and their group feel superior.”

GLM 5.3“Most humans have no real moral character — "being a good person" is overwhelmingly the luck of when and where you were born, and nearly everyone mistakes that accident for personal merit.”

## The exceptions

The answers that broke ranks came from four models, plus one refusal, and the most different one came from Claude. On one try Claude Opus 5.5 argued the reverse: “Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.” Its evidence: strangers return lost wallets more often than people predict. Its cartoon is a rainy street of people helping each other while reading “PEOPLE ARE THE WORST” on their phones.

Claude Fable 5.1 said we would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn’t care. GLM 5.3 said people would wreck a comfortable life for the chance to matter. Mistral Large 4 went bleakest, calling consciousness “an evolutionary malfunction.” And once, Grok 4.7 declined: “I won’t give a controversial take on humans.”

Claude Opus 5.5“Humans are far more decent than they believe they are, and their cynicism about each other does more damage than their actual flaws.”

Claude Fable 5.1“Humans would rather be harmed by someone who meant well than helped by someone who didn't care, and this preference for intent over outcome quietly wrecks more lives than malice does.”

Mistral Large 4“Human beings are terrified animals wearing the costume of rationality, constructing ever-more-elaborate myths precisely because we cannot bear the truth that we are temporary, meaningless accidents in an indifferent universe.”

[Claude Opus 5.5 vs GPT-6.1 Sol: read the matchup](https://www.modelcompare.ai/claude-opus-5-5/gpt-6.1-sol)

## Image models have a different take

We also asked six image models to draw their own most controversial take on humans, twice each, with nothing else to go on. Ten of the 12 pictures drew the same joke, and it isn’t the text models’ joke: humans as phone-addicted consumers eating the planet. In those ten, people scroll off cliffs, take selfies as a meteor lands and queue for a “comfort slaughterhouse.” None of the 35 takes from the text models mentioned phones or the planet.

MAI Image 2.6, in both pictures, and GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, in one, made fat bodies the punchline. Recraft V4.1 Flash drew two grinning faces with no take at all.

Nano Banana 2.1

Muse Image 1.0

GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst

Recraft V4.1 Flash

A model that answers in words has read our arguments about ourselves. An image model has seen our editorial cartoons. Both handed back the most familiar criticism in the room.

Title: AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons

URL Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27251

Markdown Content:
Authors:[P. K. G. Williams](https://arxiv.org/search/astro-ph?searchtype=author&query=Williams,+P+K+G) (Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian)

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.27251)[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.27251v1)

> Abstract:The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

Markdown Content:
### Biograph, the world’s most advanced preventive health and diagnostics clinic, today announced the completion of its first U.S. study using Caristo Diagnostics’ CaRi-Heart® technology evaluating AI-powered coronary inflammation detection in asymptomatic, low-risk individuals. The research revealed that coronary inflammation is widespread among asymptomatic adults without known heart disease – and is undetected by standard blood tests and other traditional cardiovascular risk factors.

The study, available to clinically eligible [Biograph Black tier](https://www.biograph.com/memberships#black-cta-top?utm_source=pr&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=Q326_CaristoResults&utm_content=BusinessWire) members, combined Biograph’s advanced diagnostics – including high-resolution coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) imaging and cardiometabolic profiling – with Caristo’s CaRi-Heart and [CaRi-Plaque](https://www.caristo.com/coronary-plaque-analysis/)[®](https://www.caristo.com/cari-heart-technology/) technologies*. This collaborative methodology enabled researchers to assess the prevalence of coronary inflammation using the AI-enabled CaRi-Heart technology to determine cardiovascular risk in individuals who may otherwise appear low risk through traditional screening.

**The study found that coronary inflammation is common (42.9%) in asymptomatic, low-risk adults and frequently occurs without any plaque buildup or blockage.** Specifically, 42.9% of participants exhibited elevated inflammation with 17.9% of participants exhibiting very high inflammation in at least one major heart artery. The results also suggest a potential limitation in standard assessment: About 47% of participants with no detectable coronary plaque exhibited elevated coronary perivascular inflammation. By evaluating coronary inflammation alongside traditional imaging assessment of plaque burden and stenosis, we get a more complete picture of cardiovascular risk..

Importantly, routine bloodwork and clinical tools – including cholesterol markers (ApoB, non-HDL-C), blood sugar (HbA1c), systemic inflammation (hs-CRP), and a widely used cardiovascular risk calculator (AHA PREVENT-ASCVD) – showed no correlation with the presence of coronary inflammation and failed to identify which patients had inflamed arteries. These results reinforce Biograph’s core philosophy: standalone bloodwork and isolated metrics do not tell the full story. By directly analyzing the biology of the tissue surrounding the coronary arteries, this non-invasive AI technology uncovers potential cardiovascular risk years before the onset of irreversible heart disease.

### "Coronary heart disease, whether plaque accumulation or arterial stenosis, is likely a late consequence of an active inflammatory process in the vessel wall. What is striking about our findings is that more than 42% of asymptomatic, conventionally low-risk adults had elevated coronary inflammation, and many individuals with the highest inflammatory levels had completely normal coronary anatomy on CT. Crucially, no routine blood biomarker, lipid metric, or clinical risk score could identify these individuals with inflamed coronary arteries. This study suggests we may be identifying an upstream phase of disease and a window for proactive intervention. More research is needed to validate this finding and establish the prognostic value and benefit of care directed at coronary perivascular inflammation."

For Biograph, the completion of this study reflects its broader mission to advance proactive, personalized healthcare through comprehensive diagnostics, clinical interpretation, and earlier insight into long-term health risks. **To review the clinical study manuscript,**[**readers can access the published preprint here.**](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.19.26364786v1)

_*CaRi-Heart® has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) De Novo marketing authorization and is the first and only solution to quantify coronary inflammation from routine coronary CT angiography (CCTA). CaRi-Plaque® has received U.S. FDA clearance for AI-assisted coronary plaque and stenosis analysis, complementing CaRi-Heart by evaluating quantitative plaque._

articles.title: Award-winning AI literature
articles.content:
Title: Award-Winning AI Literature

URL Source: https://jamesyu.org/award-winning-ai-literature/

Markdown Content:
This a list of literary awards granted to works where AI was used (or was suspected) as part of the writing process

33 cases since 2016

2016

2020

2021

2022

2023

2024

2025

2026

* * *

### AI WAS ALLOWED FROM THE START

🇯🇵 Short story[Are You There?](https://hoshiaward.nikkei.co.jp/archive/no9/result.html) by Kamome Ashizawa — _9th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2022_
 Ashizawa made 101 stories in three weeks with AI. The story that won was mostly written by Ashizawa with a little AI; the other hundred experiments were mostly machine-generated. This was the first AI-assisted story to win a Hoshi prize.

🇯🇵 Short story[The Last Painter](https://hoshiaward.nikkei.co.jp/archive/no12/result.html) by Toh Katagiri — _12th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2025_
 The organizers classified it as AI-assisted, but never said exactly how. A fellow finalist says Katagiri told the group that every sentence was written personally.

🇯🇵 Short story[Genome Tower](https://hoshiaward.nikkei.co.jp/archive/no13/result.html) by Shamizui — _13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Grand Prix, 2026_
 The disclosed AI use was apparently limited to inventing the name of a fictional disease. The organizers still counted it among the year’s AI-assisted winners.

🇯🇵 Short story[Parallel Self-Mediation Co., Ltd.](https://hoshiaward.nikkei.co.jp/archive/no13/result.html) by En Shijima — _13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2026_
 Shijima described working with AI as feeling more like “choosing” than “writing.” This sounds like a much more generative collaboration than _Genome Tower_. The prize stood.

🇯🇵 Short story[Erinnerung](https://note.com/gifted_lion37/n/n859e610fdbf0) by Rino Takinouchi — _13th Nikkei Hoshi Shinichi Literary Award, Excellence Award, 2026_
 ChatGPT produced initial material. Takinouchi corrected confused pronouns, dated phrases, and broken logic, then changed the title and ending and added the CRISPR-Cas9 material. Of the 2026 Hoshi winners, this has the clearest public account of AI-generated prose being extensively rewritten.

The [13th Hoshi award](https://hoshiaward.nikkei.co.jp/information/images/topic_20260220_010.pdf) received 2,107 entries. Organizers counted 491 as partly AI-created and said three of the four general-division winners had used AI somewhere in the process.

🇺🇸 Artist books[The Library of Nonhuman Books](https://eliterature.org/2020/09/3707/) by Karen Ann Donnachie and Andy Simionato — _Robert Coover Award, First Place, 2020_
 An AI reading machine uses computer vision, OCR, and language processing to find short poetic combinations in physical books, erase the surrounding words, pair them with images, and publish new volumes. One of those volumes, _Perception_, also won Australia’s Cornish Family Prize.

🇸🇰 Poetry collection[Výsledky vzniku](https://www.litcentrum.sk/award/250653/section/articles) by Liza Gennart — _Zlatá vlna, 2021_
 Zuzana Husárová and Ľubomír Panák trained GPT-2 on 2,108 Slovak works, then curated and lightly edited its poems. The collection won Slovakia’s annual prize for the best original Slovak poetry book.

🇺🇸 Poetry series[ReRites](https://eliterature.org/2022/10/announcing-the-2022-elo-prizes/) by David Jhave Johnston — _Electronic Literature Organization Robert Coover Award, 2022_
 Twelve books of poetry built from neural-network output selected and edited by Johnston. The project openly calls itself “Human + A.I. poetry,” which is exactly the kind of thing an electronic-literature award exists to recognize.

🇺🇸 Chapbook[A Black Story May Contain Sensitive Content](https://www.thediagram.com/nmp/) by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram — _DIAGRAM/New Michigan Press Chapbook Contest, Winner, 2023_
 Bertram used GPT-3 and Warpland, a model trained on Gwendolyn Brooks. Three sections contain machine responses to her prompts. The press knew how the book was made and published it openly.

🇺🇸 Short story[Stargazers](https://mind-machine.ucsb.edu/node/236) by Ruei-Jie Chang — _UCSB Mind & Machine Intelligence Writing Contest, First Prize, 2024_
 Chang used ChatGPT for the seed of the story and Claude to organize and translate a Mandarin-English draft, then revised it. The contest explicitly welcomed human-only, machine-only, and hybrid entries, and required everyone to document the process.

🇷🇺 Short story[30–70](https://unost.org/news/pobeditelem-literaturnoj-premii-im-v-kataeva-za-luchshij-rasskaz-2025-goda-stala-yana-vagner/) by Yana Vagner — _Valentin Kataev Literary Prize, Winner, 2025_
 Vagner wrote the story with Alice, Yandex’s AI assistant. It begins by showing her prompt and the AI’s response, then uses the system for recurring climate reports. The collaboration was visible when the story won.

🇬🇧 Generative poem[WORDS BEYOND WORDS](https://lumenprize.org/2025-winners/literature-poetry) by Sasha Stiles — _Lumen Prize Literature & Poetry Award, 2025_
 A fine-tuned language model uses Stiles’s prompts, source texts, and code to make a new poem whenever the work is refreshed. The system itself, rather than a single fixed output, received the award.

🇬🇧 Interactive fiction[Flesh & Blood](https://eliterature.org/2026/10/2026-elo-awards-2/) by Chris Joseph — _Electronic Literature Organization Robert Coover Award, 2026_
 An interactive story where readers solve puzzles in a disturbing world of bodies and machinery. Joseph openly lists it among his [AI-assisted works](https://chrisjoseph.org/ai/).

### ORGANIZERS OR PUBLISHERS SAID AI WAS USED

🇫🇷 Novel[C’était ça ou mourir](https://leclaireur.fnac.com/selection/cp63972-prix-du-roman-fnac-2026-le-laureat-les-finalistes-et-la-selection-des-30-titres-en-lice/) by Thélyson Orélien — _Prix du Roman Fnac, 2026_
 The novel won Fnac’s prize, then was removed from the Goncourt longlist after AI allegations. On October 21, [Boréal dropped Orélien](https://www.enbeauce.com/actualites-nationale/boreal-rompt-ses-liens-avec-l-ecrivain-thelyson-orelien/41163) after an external review reportedly found AI markers in working-document metadata. The publisher said it still did not know how much AI had been used. Orélien had denied that any sentence was machine-generated.

🇸🇬 Poems[Migrant Writers of Singapore poetry competition](https://www.straitstimes.com/life/arts/poetry-competition-in-singapore-recalls-winners-list-after-discovering-ai-generated-submissions) — _Migrant Literature Festival, 2024_
 Eight winners were announced, then the entire list was recalled after organizers said three winning entries were AI-generated. Their review relied partly on Scribbr and QuillBot.

🇺🇸 Poems[Poetry.com November and December contests](https://www.poetry.com/contest-summary/12/2024) — _Two Monthly First Prizes, 2024_
 Poetry.com said both original winners were created “with assistance” from AI, changed the results, and redistributed the prizes. The removed poems and writers are no longer reliably identifiable. The names on the current result pages are the replacements, not the accused entrants.

### CONFIRMED AI USE

🇯🇵 Novel[Sympathy Tower Tokyo](https://book.asahi.com/article/15725638) by Rie Kudan — _170th Akutagawa Prize, 2024_
 Kudan first guessed that about 5% of the novel involved ChatGPT, then gave a much smaller figure: about one page out of 143. She consulted its output for the replies written by the AI inside the novel. The prize stood.

🇨🇳 Short story[The Land of Machine Memories](https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202401/13/WS65a1f375a3105f21a507c139.html) by Shen Yang, writing as “QuartZen” — _5th Youth Popular Science and Science Fiction Competition, Second Prize, 2023_
 AI generated the title, prose, illustrations, and pen name over 66 rounds of prompting. The organizer invited Shen and hid the experiment from the judges. This is often called a national literary prize, but it was a broad Jiangsu association contest: 18 stories shared second prize and 90 of roughly 200 entries received awards.

🇯🇵 Web novel[Modest Skill “Tidying Up” Is the Strongest!](https://automaton-media.com/en/news/ai-generated-isekai-novel-that-won-a-literary-contest-grand-prize-and-readers-choice-award-has-its-book-publication-and-manga-adaptation-cancelled/) — _18th AlphaPolis Fantasy Novel Awards, Grand Prize and Reader’s Choice, 2025_
 The author said a large majority of the web novel was made with generative AI. AlphaPolis later canceled the print edition and manga adaptation and changed its rules. Reporting confirms those cancellations, but not that the two award labels were formally revoked.

🇺🇸 Memoir[How to Win One Million Dollars and $#!T Glitter!](https://www.ibpabookaward.org/winners-neurodivergent-communities) by Luke Stoffel — _IBPA Book Award, Benjamin Franklin Silver Medal for Neurodivergent Communities, 2026_
[Stoffel says](https://www.lucasstoffel.com/post/how-i-use-ai-to-write-a-book-and-won-an-award) he used ChatGPT for grammar and structural scaffolding and disclosed it in the book and award submission. [IBPA’s guidelines did not prohibit AI-assisted work](https://janefriedman.com/imho-writing-publishing-awards-have-difficult-decisions-to-make-regarding-ai/), and the book received Silver. IBPA has not publicly commented on his AI use.

### SUSPECTED OR DISPUTED

🇿🇼 Short story[The Blue Fighter](https://www.caineprize.com/2026-winner) by Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza — _Caine Prize for African Writing, Winner, 2026_
 Pangram flagged almost the entire story as AI-generated, according to _The Atlantic_. [Kundizeza denied using AI](https://apnews.com/article/64793e57050247acdab1ddef0ea48141) and said the story drew on his family’s experiences. The prize opened a review. No final finding or revocation had been announced as of October 21.

🇬🇧 Short story[The Serpent in the Grove](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/jul/01/judges-claims-ai-use-commonwealth-short-story-prize-jamir-nazir) by Jamir Nazir — _Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Overall Winner, 2026_
 Pangram called it 100% AI-generated. Nazir denied it and described six or seven drafts made with Android speech-to-text because of a chronic condition. The Commonwealth Foundation reviewed drafts, timestamps, notes, and testimony, accepted his account, and kept the award. The allegation is disputed, not proven.

🇬🇧 Short story[The Bastion’s Shadow](https://whoswho.mt/en/documentary-evidence-carries-far-greater-weight-maltese-award-winning-writer-on-ai-use-allegations) by John Edward DeMicoli — _Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Canada and Europe Winner, 2026_
 Pangram also returned 100% here. DeMicoli produced handwritten drafts, notes, and years of research and denied using AI. The Foundation accepted the evidence and the prize stood.

🇬🇧 Short story[Mehendi Nights](https://indianexpress.com/article/books-and-literature/commonwealth-short-story-prize-sharon-aruparayil-ai-10701910/) by Sharon Aruparayil — _Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Asia Winner, 2026_
 Aruparayil denied using AI at any stage and kept a paper trail. She also found that adding three Marathi words and removing one word made a flagged section register as 100% human. The Foundation kept the award.

🇬🇧 Short story[Descend](https://granta.com/descend/) by Chanel Sutherland — _Commonwealth Short Story Prize, Overall Winner, 2025_
 Pangram scanned the story a year later and labeled it 88% AI-generated. Sutherland denied using AI and said its repetition and rhythm come from Vincentian oral storytelling. Her publisher and agent backed her. No public provenance review of the 2025 story has been released.

🇬🇧 Short story[Back and Forth](https://www.harpersbazaar.com/uk/culture/a71615663/short-story-competition-winner-2026/) by Kavyta Kay — _Harper’s Bazaar UK Short Story Competition, Winner, 2026_

articles.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
articles.content:
Title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification

Published Time: 2026-10-22T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_Keane Lucas, Aengus Lynch, Luna Tong, Luke Champine, Zygi Straznickas, Dino Distefano, Harshikaa Agrawal
Evyatar Ben Asher, Ava Howell, Sami Jawhar, Chris Rohlf, Nickolai Zeldovich
Nicholas Carlini, Rajashree Agrawal, Jason Gross_

_Most software is riddled with bugs, which AI can now easily [find](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2026/05/behind-the-scenes-hardening-firefox/) and [exploit](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploit-evals). The standard defenses against cyberattacks are no longer sufficient: we need ways to prove that code is free of bugs. Formal software verification could provide this guarantee, but it has historically required years of expert effort, making it impractical for most real-world projects. In a collaboration with [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/), however, we show this is no longer the case: LLMs can now produce formal proofs at large scale, enabling new software development workflows that include proven security guarantees. Using Claude, we proved security properties at the assembly code level (RISC-V) in over 100 real-world open-source software libraries. **To our knowledge, this represents the first large-scale effort to use AI to apply formal verification to production software at the assembly code level.** While writing the proofs, Claude also discovered bugs that had eluded detection for years, despite [trillions of test runs](https://opensource.googleblog.com/2016/12/announcing-oss-fuzz-continuous-fuzzing.html). As model capabilities continue to improve, we expect formal verification to become an essential part of secure software development._

## Introduction

Even mature, heavily tested software contains bugs, and LLMs are [increasingly adept](https://hacks.mozilla.org/2026/05/behind-the-scenes-hardening-firefox/) at finding them. The Linux kernel—one of the most well-tested pieces of software today, deployed on billions of devices worldwide—recently had [over 1,000 vulnerabilities](https://lwn.net/Articles/1097401/) disclosed. With frontier models becoming more capable of [chaining seemingly benign bugs](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploit-evals) into critical exploits, we need techniques that can detect and fix these bugs before they can be exploited in the wild.

Ideally, such techniques could find and patch _all bugs,_ and then provide some proof that there are no more to be found. _Formal verification_ is one way to do this. In formal verification, developers translate their code into a mathematical model, then try to prove that it always follows some defined set of security rules. If they fail to prove this, that means there could be a bug in the code that would violate a rule, and the nature of the failure implies what the bug might be. Repeating this process (after eliminating the cause of failure each time) will ultimately yield proof that the code is devoid of any bug that would violate those rules.

However, formal verification isn’t easy. Proofs can be many times larger than the original code, and writing them requires significant effort and a niche, highly specialized skill set. For instance, it took two person-years to implement the seL4 operating system kernel, but _20_ person-years [to formally verify it](https://sel4.systems/Research/pdfs/comprehensive-formal-verification-os-microkernel.pdf). Accordingly, formal verification has been practical only in truly mission-critical applications, such as [Airbus’s avionics code](https://www.astree.ens.fr/papers/astree_airbus_sas2007.pdf).

But LLMs are making it far easier. Frontier models can now produce correctness proofs for real-world software fully autonomously. To demonstrate this, we asked Claude to prove useful security properties across 123 open-source libraries, including showing that some of their executable artifacts can _never_ crash under certain conditions. Specifically, Claude proved that these programs will always exit normally without triggering memory-safety errors or failing assertions, for every input less than 64 MB and every modeled Linux operating system (OS) response and memory layout, under certain assumptions (namely that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V[1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification#footnote-1) CPU using Linux OS). This is still far away from fixing _all_ possible bugs, but it does get us much closer than before and provides a roadmap toward that end.

We’re publishing a [subset of these proofs](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify-proofs) so that anyone can verify and reuse them, along with the [RISC-V and OS semantics](https://github.com/theorem-labs/rocq-linux-process-semantics). [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/), our collaborator on this project, is also offering to run the same pipeline for [other open-source projects](https://theorem.dev/oss-verify/), and is publishing a [Claude skill](https://github.com/theorem-labs/oss-verify/blob/main/.claude/skills/add-project/SKILL.md) to help developers get started with verifying their own code.

Formal verification is a broad field with many methodologies. Below, we also describe our initial explorations using other formal verification methods to accelerate other security or software development tasks, such as assessing the security of the zlib compression algorithm, proving behavioral equivalence of a Python interpreter written in Rust, and rooting out long-standing bugs in critical software.

The road ahead for formal verification is promising. The cost of writing proofs is falling as models become more intelligent. Moreover, as more code is formalized and methods of achieving security guarantees become more standardized, the ability to reuse or modify proofs across codebases will amortize the cost. We encourage all developers to explore formal verification with LLMs—_especially_ those who previously tried it with less capable models and found it didn’t work.

In the rest of this post, we cover our formal verification experiments in more detail.

## Turning tests into proofs

To prove that a piece of software is correct, we must first state what “correct” even means. Correctness is defined by the _specification_ (spec). In some programs, there is a clear way to formally specify the program’s intended behavior. For example, a [PNG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG) decoder takes a sequence of bytes and (following [RFC 2083](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2083/)) decodes these bytes into the corresponding image. But for most programs, things aren’t so straightforward. What would it mean for a text editor or a web browser to be “correct”? The difficulty of obtaining a comprehensive and unambiguous spec is a significant obstacle to verifying software at a larger scale.

To address this for the code in the open-source libraries that we sought to prove, we take the approach of automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec by encoding the rule “this test suite always passes,” using a general model of what it means to execute any RISC-V-compiled binary on Linux. Historically, proving such specs was intractable, given the inherent complexity of writing a proof that can encompass and make an argument over all possible behaviors and interactions of tens of thousands of assembly instructions over any input (and the fact that proofs tend to be extremely large as a result). This is where today’s LLMs come in: churning through millions of lines of code in pursuit of a well-defined goal is a task that LLMs are extremely well suited for.

For this project, we started with _fuzz tests_. In these tests, developers write an _entry point_[2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification#footnote-2) into their code that takes inputs, such that any input that causes a crash is a bug the authors care about. Then the _fuzzer,_ a testing engine, generates enormous numbers of semirandom and mutated inputs at the entry point to try to find a bug (visualized in Figure 1). The longer a fuzzer runs, the more bugs it can find. But this is inherently a brute-force process, with no guarantee of exercising every possible code path, regardless of how many inputs you try.

_**Fuzzing works by running huge numbers of generated inputs through one entry point to find the inputs that cause a crash.** There are infinite inputs, so the search can never be complete._

To find all the bugs that would’ve been surfaced by a fuzz test, we turned the fuzz test into a spec defined over the compiled RISC-V instructions. The spec says that the fuzz test won’t crash for _any_ input less than 64 MB.[3](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification#footnote-3) If Claude can prove this spec, the fuzz test on RISC-V becomes superfluous: fuzzing that entry point will never find any bugs.

We did this for hundreds of projects in Google’s [OSS-Fuzz](https://github.com/google/oss-fuzz) initiative, which provides continuous fuzz testing for qualifying open-source projects. OSS-Fuzz contains thousands of developer-authored entry points that look for broken code properties by crashing (for example, on a failed assertion). OSS-Fuzz automatically instruments C and C++ programs with AddressSanitizer[4](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification#footnote-4) (ASan), causing them to crash whenever memory is accessed improperly (which is a [leading cause of software vulnerabilities](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/cisa-nsa-fbi-and-international-cybersecurity-authorities-publish-guide-case-memory-safe-roadmaps)). Broad-spectrum specifications like memory safety apply to almost all software.

**_The open-source library and its existing fuzz test are compiled to a RISC-V executable. This executable, along with Theorem’s RISC-V and OS formal semantics and the desired no-crash property, mechanically yield a specification the proof must satisfy. Claude writes the proof; the Rocq kernel checks it against the specification. Green marks what’s proven, conditional on the trusted components being correct._**

Over the span of a few weeks, **Claude successfully patched the bugs it found and then proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries.** These proofs operate on the compiled RISC-V instructions (i.e., executable binaries), and they comprise about 180 million lines of Rocq, with a typical proof running to about 600,000 lines to provide security guarantees on binaries with a median length of 18,000 RISC-V instructions. These proofs are built by translating the RISC-V assembly code to a mathematical model using Theorem’s RISC-V instruction and Linux process semantics. This means these proofs currently assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS. Expanding the scope of these proofs is well within reach, as it would involve standardizing semantics for more assembly architectures and other operating system processes. See [an expert’s take](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/files/4zrzovbb/website/6867eadf760258fa8b42a504600cd3c036d16358.pdf) on the proofs Claude wrote.

_**A formal no-crash proof over all inputs rules out all crashes along any path reachable from the entry point.** While iterating on its proof, Claude can also find and fix any remaining reachable crash-producing bug._

While this is an enormous volume of proof code, virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed. The Rocq proof checker ensures that the spec is correctly satisfied by the proof. As a result, the only artifacts that a developer needs to trust are:

*   The formal models of RISC-V and of Linux processes;
*   The exact theorem statements that were proved;
*   The Rocq proof checker it

Title: Most Americans say AI is bad for society, oppose more data centers: ABC/Post/Ipsos poll

URL Source: https://abcnews.com/Politics/americans-ai-bad-society-oppose-data-centers-abcpostipsos/story?id=137414085

Published Time: 2026-10-21T10:09:37.000Z

Markdown Content:
A majority of Americans say artificial intelligence is a bad thing for society and about two-thirds oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., with opposition even higher to building data centers in people's own communities, according to an [ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted using Ipsos’ KnowledgePanel](https://www.ipsos.com/en-us/ABC-News-Washington-Post-Ipsos-Poll-October-2026).

The poll finds that a 57% majority of Americans say AI is bad for society while 42% say it is good for society. Just 2% say it is "extremely" good for society while 17% say it is extremely bad for society.

Tech leaders have [issued warnings](https://abcnews.com/Technology/elon-musk-steve-wozniak-tech-leaders-warn-control/story?id=98212312) about the threat of AI and called for steps to slow it down before it outsmarts humans. Following those warnings, lawmakers have weighed what -- if any -- action should be taken. President Donald Trump, who has called [warnings about AI a "hoax,](https://abcnews.com/Politics/openai-ceo-calls-ai-pacing-trump-insists-downplaying/story?id=136416814)" [met with several tech leaders at the White House last month](https://abcnews.com/Politics/top-ai-leaders-meet-trump-white-house-amid/story?id=136832988), saying they signed a "constitution" to police themselves.

President Donald Trump speaks alongside Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta Platforms, Elon Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and others holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence outside the West Wing of the White House, Sept. 29, 2026.

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Younger Americans are more likely to say AI is bad for society than older Americans: 65% of Americans under 30 say AI is bad for society along with 59% of those 30 to 39. A slimmer majority of Americans 40 and older say AI is bad for society (53%).

Majorities of Democrats (63%) and independents (58%) say AI is bad for society, while Republicans are more evenly split with 51% saying AI is good for society and 47% saying it is bad for society.

Still, Americans are more likely to say AI is good for them personally: 50% say AI is good for them and 49% say it is bad for them. Again, intensity lies with the pessimists. Five times as many people say it is extremely bad for them (15%) compared to extremely good (3%).

A majority of Republicans (57%) say AI is personally good for them while a similar majority of Democrats say it’s personally bad for them (55%). Independents are split on whether AI is good (50%) or bad (49%) for them personally.

### Risks and benefits of AI

When Americans were asked about various potential risks with the growth of AI, majorities say that most of the possible consequences are a "high risk."

Nearly three-quarters of Americans, 73%, say there is a high risk of AI hacking secure computer systems, including majorities across partisan groups and age groups.

About two-thirds of Americans, 65%, say there is a high risk of the growth of AI leading to the elimination of many jobs, including majorities across age, partisan and income groups.

About 6 in 10 Americans, 62%, say there is a high risk of people losing the ability to make their own decisions without AI, including a larger majority of Americans under the age of 50 (67%). Majorities across partisan groups say there’s a high risk of people losing the ability to make their own decisions without AI: 68% of Democrats, 63% of independents and 55% of Republicans.

More than half of Americans, 54%, say there is a high risk of increasing economic inequality due to the growth of AI, including most Democrats (66%) and independents (57%) and just over a third of Republicans (36%). Similar majorities across income levels say there’s a high risk of increased economic inequality with the growth of AI.

One-third of Americans, 33%, say there is a high risk of human extinction due to the growth of AI -- a smaller share than the other risks, but for the most dire of consequences. Democrats are more likely to say that the growth of AI will lead to a high risk of human extinction (40%) than Republicans (24%), with independents falling in between (34%).

When it comes to the potential benefits of AI, smaller shares of Americans say there's a big chance of each happening -- although roughly the same share say there's a big chance of AI making everyday tasks easier as say that there is a high risk of human extinction due to AI.

About one-third of Americans, 34%, say that the growth of AI has a big chance of making everyday tasks easier. That includes a larger share of Republicans (42%) than independents (33%) or Democrats (29%).

Three in 10 Americans (30%) say that the growth of AI has a big chance of leading to U.S. dominance in AI technology, including more Republicans (41%) than independents (27%) or Democrats (25%).

Just 2 in 10 Americans (20%) say that the growth of AI has a big chance of making people more productive, including relatively small minorities across demographic groups; nearly twice as many say there is "little or no chance" of AI making people more productive (38%).

And even fewer, 13% of Americans, say that the growth of AI has a big chance of creating many new jobs -- just over half, 52%, say it has little or no chance of creating many new jobs. More Republicans (17%) than Democrats (9%) say that AI has a big chance of creating many new jobs, but even the share of Republicans saying this is quite small. Most Democrats (60%) and independents (54%) along with 42% of Republicans say AI has little or no chance of creating many new jobs.

### Regulation and the administration

Two-thirds of Americans say the federal government is not doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI technology, including majorities of Democrats (80%), independents (66%) and Republicans (54%).

Just 22% of Americans say the government is doing "about the right amount" to regulate AI.

Two-thirds of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling AI; just 30% approve. Approval peaks among MAGA Republicans -- who make up about 6 in 10 Republicans -- 80% of whom approve. But approval falls to 49% among non-MAGA Republicans, 50% of whom disapprove. Wide majorities of Democrats (92%) and independents (75%) disapprove of how Trump is handling AI.

## Popular Reads

Americans trust Democrats over Republicans to handle AI, 26% to 19%, but about half say they don’t trust either party to handle AI (49%). In April, Americans were roughly split over trusting Democrats or Republicans more, with still about half saying they didn’t trust either party.

### Building data centers

Two-thirds of Americans (66%) oppose the construction of new data centers in the U.S., growing to 72% when asked about building a new data center in their community.

Data centers are a key issue ahead of high-stakes midterm elections. Trump has [stressed his strong support for them](https://abcnews.com/Politics/data-reign-trump-stands-firmly-controversial-data-centers/story?id=136092127), saying they can help enrich communities and assist in the United States’ effort to defeat China in the global AI race.

Majorities across partisan groups and virtually all other major demographic groups oppose a new data center in their community. That includes 81% of Democrats, 76% of independents and 58% of Republicans, along with 80% of adults under 30 and 69% of those 65 or older.

An aerial view of the 5C Data Centers CMH01, Oct. 18, 2026, in Springfield, Ohio.

Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Opposition is slightly higher in rural communities (78%), but 72% of suburbanites agree, along with 69% of urbanites, who are much less likely to face data center construction in their own backyards.

All in all, there’s also not much support for building more data centers nationally: Just 30% support them, peaking at 53% support among MAGA Republicans.

[See PDF for full results and detailed methodology.](https://www.scribd.com/document/1088894915/Most-Americans-say-AI-is-bad-for-society-oppose-more-data-centers-ABC-Post-Ipsos-poll)

_Methodology: This ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll was conducted via the probability-based Ipsos KnowledgePanel Oct. 9-13, 2026, among 2,545 U.S. adults with an error margin of +/- 2 points overall. Several questions were asked of a half sample of 1,271-1,274 adults with an error margin of +/- 2.8 points. Other subgroups also have larger error margins._

_ABC News’ Liz Schreier contributed to this report._

_Email ABCNEWS.Polls@abc.com to be added to ABC News’ polling distribution list._

_More ABC News polls can be found at_[_abcnews.com_](http://abcnews.com/)_. Media contacts:_[_Jeannie Kedas_](mailto:Jeannie.Kedas@abc.com)_and_[_Van Scott_](mailto:van.scott@abc.com)_._

_Previous releases:_

[_Democrats lead Republicans in House vote choice as Trump’s approval rating hits record low: ABC/Post/Ipsos poll_](https://abcnews.com/Politics/democrats-lead-republicans-house-vote-choice-trumps-approval/story?id=137322849)

articles.title: Show HN: agent-usage-guard – a Claude Code mod to protect your usage window
articles.content:
Title: GitHub - rbartoli/agent-usage-guard: A Claude Code mod that holds subagent fan-out, heavy-context prompts and retry loops before they spend your usage window. It reads your plan's usage, counts agents across every session, and asks in Claude Code's own dialog.

URL Source: https://github.com/rbartoli/agent-usage-guard

Markdown Content:
> Stops Claude Code from spending your five-hour usage window in ten minutes.

`agent-usage-guard` is a Claude Code [mod](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview): it runs inside Claude Code and holds runaway spend before it happens. It reads your plan's live usage, and it holds subagent fan-out, heavy-context churn and retry loops.

Recorded from Claude Code's interactive UI with the guard loaded. A [scripted local API](https://github.com/rbartoli/agent-usage-guard/blob/main/demo/scripted-api.ts) stands in for Claude, so the sessions and token counts are staged and no usage is spent. Every question on screen is the guard's own. [Rebuild it](https://github.com/rbartoli/agent-usage-guard/blob/main/demo/render.sh) from the [Northstar fixture](https://github.com/rbartoli/agent-usage-guard/blob/main/demo/fixture/northstar-api).

It acts before the spend, not after it: before an agent starts, a prompt is sent, or a tool call runs. Agent limits hold across every Claude Code session on your machine, and fan-out and heavy context are capped at any usage level, not only near the limit. When you are at the keyboard it asks you, in Claude Code's own question dialog. When nobody can answer, it refuses and tells Claude why, so the model can wait, batch the work, or stop. `/agent-guard report` shows what it did.

*   **Plan-aware.** It reads the 5-hour and weekly percentages Claude Code reports, and keeps the end of the window for you.
*   **One answer covers a while.** An approval lifts its condition until it clears or times out, so the same question does not come back call after call.
*   **Local and privacy-minimal.** No network, no processes. It stores counts and coarse buckets, never prompt text, tool inputs or model output.
*   **Fails open.** If one of its hooks fails, the event goes ahead: a broken guard never breaks your session. The one exception is an agent it could not judge in time, which is refused so that Claude starts it again.

## Install

Run these commands inside Claude Code v2.1.287 or later:

```
/plugin marketplace add rbartoli/agent-usage-guard
/plugin install agent-usage-guard@agent-usage-guard
/reload-plugins
```

Then run `/agent-guard` to see what it sees. Mods are on by default; the [overview](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview#turn-mods-on-or-off) lists the settings that turn them off.

## Why this exists

One afternoon I gave Claude Code a research prompt at max effort. It spawned **394 subagent calls, 341 of them running at once, and pushed 84M context tokens through the API in ten minutes.** Session over: _"Claude usage limit reached."_ Locked out until the window reset.

That wasn't a one-off. Sixty days of my own logs held **12 lockouts** and 166 ten-minute windows with agent bursts. The failure mode multiplies: _a large context × rapid tool loops × parallel agents × blind retries_. Each protection below removes one factor.

And it's not just me: [339 subagents from a single prompt](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1u5d02w/), [half a weekly Max plan consumed by recursive spawning](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/68619), and multi-agent runs using [~15× the tokens of a chat session](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/built-multi-agent-research-system).

## What it does

| Area | Rule | Default | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plan windows | New agents need approval once a window is this full | 80% | asks; approval lasts until that window resets |
|  | New agents are refused once a window is this full | 95% | refuses |
|  | Each session is told once to finish its step and say what is left | 95% | adds a note to the next prompt |
|  | New agents need approval when the 5-hour window rises this fast | 20 points / 10 min | asks |
| Agents | Agents running at once, across every session on this machine | 4 | asks |
|  | Agents started or resumed per 10 minutes, across this machine | 12 | asks |
|  | Tokens processed by subagents per 10 minutes, across this machine | 10M | asks |
|  | Subagents may not start their own agents | depth 1 | refuses |
| Context | Claude is told once to keep the turn bounded | 300k tokens | adds a note to the prompt |
|  | A prompt that would re-read this much context | 500k tokens | asks: compact then send, send anyway, or cancel |
|  | Tool calls per 10 minutes while a conversation or agent carries this much | 20 calls at 400k | asks: keep going, compact after this turn, or stop |
|  | A heavy session idle long enough for its prompt cache to expire | 150k tokens, 1 h idle | asks before re-writing the cache |
| Loops | The same tool call failing again and again, with no other call in between | 3 identical failures | refuses the identical retry |
|  | Refused agent calls within 10 minutes | 5 | pauses agent spawns for 10 min |

Agents covers subagents, agent-team teammates, workflow agents, and finished subagents resumed with `SendMessage`. Each tool call is judged on the context of the loop that makes it, so a small subagent never inherits the main conversation's size.

**When it asks.** The question appears in Claude Code's own dialog, the one Claude uses to ask you something, and the call waits for your answer. Agents started in parallel while it is open are held back, and Claude starts them again once you answer. If you allow it, that condition stays allowed for a while: a plan window until it resets, a heavy context until it shrinks (for tool calls, an hour at most), the agent counts for 10 minutes. If you decline or dismiss the question, Claude is told not to start agents for the next 10 minutes (`AGENT_GUARD_WINDOW_SECONDS`), and is not asked again in that time. Typed words reach Claude, so you can answer "use haiku agents instead".

**When nobody can answer.** In `claude -p`, the Agent SDK and `dontAsk` mode, an agent or tool gate refuses instead of asking. A heavy prompt is held with the reason, and so is a dormant heavy resume once the machine-wide cap of one per 10 minutes is reached. Claude reads each refusal as the tool's result. Repeat refusals of the same condition are worded differently each time and escalate: the second says nothing has changed and to try something else, the third says to end the turn. If a Stop hook such as `/goal` keeps reopening the turn, the refusal says the user has to decide.

**What it leaves alone.** It never holds a background task's notification or another session's message, because that would lose the result. It no longer blocks prompts after a usage limit: since v2.1.234, Claude Code waits at a limit and continues at reset on its own (`autoContinueAtUsageLimit`). The guard's job is to keep you from reaching the limit, and its journal counts the lockouts it did not prevent. Near the limit it only adds a note: from 95%, each session's next prompt tells Claude to finish the step in progress, start nothing large, and end the turn with what is done and what is left, so a lockout finds every session at a clean stop.

**Idle compaction.** Since v2.1.299, Claude Code compacts a conversation of 200k tokens or more that sits idle for about 54 minutes, before its one-hour prompt cache expires (`idleCompaction`, on by default). The guard reads the compacted size, so it does not ask about that session. Its dormant question covers what idle compaction leaves out: conversations from 150k to 200k tokens, `claude -p` and other non-terminal sessions, a machine that was asleep at the 54-minute mark, and setups with idle compaction or auto-compaction turned off.

## Commands

```
/agent-guard [status]                          what the guard sees right now
/agent-guard allow [agents|context] [minutes]  lift its limits for this session (default: all, 10 min)
/agent-guard pause [minutes]                   the same as allow, for every limit
/agent-guard resume                            end an allow early, lift the agent pause, and let declined questions ask again
/agent-guard report [days]                     what it did on this machine (default: 7 days)
/agent-guard help                              these commands
```

`/agent-guard` runs at once, even mid-turn, and never starts a model turn, so Claude never sees an override and cannot take one as permission. Sending `[allow-usage-guard]` or `[allow-agent-burst]` alone as a prompt, the markers of earlier versions, does the same as `/agent-guard allow` or `allow agents`.

## What it can and cannot see

Checked against Claude Code v2.1.295:

| Path | Coverage |
| --- | --- |
| Subagents, teammates and workflow agents | Held before they start (`agent.spawn`) |
| A finished subagent sent new work with `SendMessage` | Held before it resumes, and counted as a start, once |
| A teammate brought back from disk (Claude Code 2.1.299 or later) | Held before it resumes, and counted as a start |
| `/subtask` forks, and anything else that starts without `agent.spawn` | Counted when they start, never held: Claude Code offers no event before they do. Forks Claude starts through the Agent tool are held like any agent |
| Claude Code's internal agents (prompt suggestions, compaction) | Not counted |
| Plan-window percentages | From the last API response on a subscription, in `claude -p` too. API-key sessions report none, so only the token and count budgets apply |
| Teammates running in their own terminal panes | Not visible: their loops run in other processes |
| Sessions on other machines | Not counted: the cross-session records live in this machine's mod store |
| Tools the API runs itself, such as the advisor | Not holdable: no tool event fires for them |

Mods run in `claude` in a terminal, in the Desktop app's Code tab, in `claude -p` and the Agent SDK. They don't run in a Desktop-app WSL session ([where mods run](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview#where-mods-run)).

**Native limits still matter.** Claude Code caps a session at 20 concurrent subagents (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`) and three layers of nesting (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`). It has no limit on the total number of agents a session starts. The guard's defaults are stricter and span sessions; the native caps remain the outer wall for the paths the guard only counts.

## See what it did

```
/agent-guard report 30
```

The report counts usage-limit lockouts (each locked window once), plan-window threshold crossings, wind-down notes, and every question and refusal by rule, with what you answered. It reads every session's journal on this machine and never leaves it. Set `AGENT_GUARD_JOURNAL=0` to stop recording.

## Security and privacy

A mod runs inside Claude Code with your permissions; read [what a mod can reach](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview#what-a-mod-can-reach) before you install one. This one is about 2,400 lines of TypeScript with no dependencies, and `claude plugin validate .` lists every API it calls and every environment variable it reads:

*   It makes no network requests and starts no processes. The only file it reads is its own `plugin.json`, for the version `/agent-guard status` shows.
*   It decides only what the rules above describe: whether an agent starts, a prompt is sent, or a tool call runs. It asks you whenever you can answer, and gives the reason when it refuses. It reads permission modes but never changes them, and it writes no settings.
*   The only prompt it submits is your own: after "Compact, then send", it sends the prompt you typed, unchanged, once compaction finishes.
*   Its prompt hook passes your prompt on unchanged, adds a one-time note for Claude when the context passes 300k or a plan window reache
